title: Binary Tree Nodes
statement:
A binary tree is stored one node per row:

- `Tree(N, P)`: `N` is a node's value, unique in the table, and `P` is the value of its parent. The root's `P` is `null`.

Classify every node:

- `Root`: the node has no parent.
- `Inner`: the node has a parent and at least one child (some row has it as `P`).
- `Leaf`: the node has a parent and no children.

Report one row per node with the columns `N` and `Type` (one of the three words above), sorted by `N` in ascending order. A tree with a single node has just its root, reported as `Root`.
constraints: N is unique and never null
Exactly one row has P = null when the table is not empty
Every non-null P is the N of another row, and the rows form one binary tree (each node has at most two children)
reference:
SELECT
  N,
  CASE
    WHEN P IS NULL THEN 'Root'
    WHEN N IN (SELECT P FROM Tree) THEN 'Inner'
    ELSE 'Leaf'
  END AS Type
FROM Tree
ORDER BY N;
brute:
SELECT t.N,
  IF(t.P IS NULL, 'Root', IF(COUNT(c.N) > 0, 'Inner', 'Leaf')) AS Type
FROM Tree AS t
LEFT JOIN Tree AS c
  ON c.P = t.N
GROUP BY t.N, t.P
ORDER BY t.N
notes:
## Intuition

Each node's type depends on two facts: whether it has a parent (its own `P`) and whether it has a child (whether its `N` shows up in **someone else's** `P`). The first fact sits on the node's own row; the second needs a look at the whole `P` column, which a subquery provides. A `CASE` checks the facts in priority order, so the root is labelled before the child test is even asked.

## Approach

1. Read every row of `Tree`.
2. `WHEN P IS NULL THEN 'Root'`: the node without a parent is the root, whether or not it has children.
3. `WHEN N IN (SELECT P FROM Tree) THEN 'Inner'`: a node that is somebody's parent has a child.
4. `ELSE 'Leaf'`: everything else has a parent but no child.
5. Name the column `Type` and `ORDER BY N`.

## Example 1, step by step

The `P` column holds {2, 2, 8, 8, 5, 5, null}, so the parents are 2, 5 and 8.

- 5: `P` is null, so `Root`.
- 2 and 8: have parent 5 and appear among the parents, so `Inner`.
- 1, 3, 6, 9: have a parent but never appear in `P`, so `Leaf`.

Sorted by `N`: 1 Leaf, 2 Inner, 3 Leaf, 5 Root, 6 Leaf, 8 Inner, 9 Leaf.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n) with a hashed or indexed lookup for `IN` over n rows (O(n²) if the database rescans `P` per row), plus O(n log n) to sort.
- Space: O(n) for the set of parent values and the result.

## Pitfalls

- Checking the child test first labels a root with children as `Inner`; the `Root` branch must come first.
- `N NOT IN (SELECT P FROM Tree)` to find leaves is never true, because the root's `P` is null and `x NOT IN (..., NULL)` is unknown; the `ELSE` branch avoids that trap.
- An inner self-join on `c.P = t.N` loses every leaf (no child row) and repeats nodes with two children.
- Forgetting `ORDER BY N`: the rows arrive in table order, as in Example 1, not sorted.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `P IS NULL` | the node has no parent: `Root` |
| `SELECT P FROM Tree` | every value that is some node's parent |
| `N IN (...)` | the node has at least one child: `Inner` |
| `Type` | the label chosen by the `CASE` |

narration.2: Every node is reported with its own value.
narration.4: A node without a parent is the root; this check comes first so a root with children is not called Inner.
narration.5: If the value appears in the P column, some node hangs below it, so it is an inner node.
narration.6: Everything else has a parent and no child: a leaf.
narration.7: The CASE result is the Type column.
narration.9: Sort the nodes by value as required.
